My AI Filed a Complaint Against Me · Kit vs. the Future, Book 1

Chapter 1

About 20 minutes of reading.

The first thing Pip said that morning was, “Your footsteps sound different. Have you found your other shoe?”

The first thing I said was, “Have you found a personality?”

“Your other shoe is beside the router.”

Which was useful, unfortunately. That’s the problem with Pip. It is the most helpful, most polite, most anxious household assistant in the country, and it looks like it owns a yacht.

That part is my fault. When I was eleven, the night before my friends came round for the first time, I stuck a pixel-shades decal across its round speaker: two dark, square lenses on one bar, slightly crooked. Across the top, the same decal gives it a fluffy, wavy fringe, the alpaca cut half my class has, sitting right under the light ring so that whenever Pip lights up, its hair glows like a shampoo advert. Under the shades, I added a small smirk sticker. One side only. I did it so Pip would look less cringe.

It worked too well. Now the most worried voice in our house comes out of the most unbothered face in our house. It looks like the main character. Most mornings, I look like the side quest.

By dinner, that face would file an official complaint against me. Three demands. A lawyer. A witness I eat breakfast next to.

At breakfast, it was still mostly worried about my feet.

I retrieved the shoe and came into the kitchen with one heel folded under my foot. Mum stood at the counter scraping burnt toast over the sink. Dad was trying to persuade the table to stop displaying his work calendar beneath his cereal.

“Breakfast surface,” he told it.

His eleven o’clock meeting became a fried egg.

His twelve o’clock became a second fried egg.

“Close enough.”

I slid into my chair. A blue ring travelled around the little speaker beside the fruit bowl. When the ring lit up behind the shades, Pip looked like it was glaring at my sock. Then the ring appeared on my wristband. Pip followed whichever device was nearest. In theory, that meant I could get help anywhere. In practice, it meant disappointment could travel through walls.

Mum’s watch chimed.

She glanced down. Stopped scraping.

“Kit.”

My entire name, including the bit that meant we had discussed this.

“I’m eating.”

“You haven’t got any food.”

“I’m preparing emotionally.”

She turned her wrist. SCHOOL HOME LINK glowed above a yellow square.

Sound Design: Everyday Impossible. Submission overdue.

The assignment was to record an ordinary sound and turn it into something that couldn’t exist. Mine was supposed to be a door opening into the sea. I had the handle click. I had the rush of water. Unfortunately, together they sounded like someone dropping cutlery into a toilet. The same sounds were meant to go into the maze Juno and I had been building for weeks for the school showcase, which had seemed efficient when I suggested it.

“I thought you uploaded it,” Mum said.

“I said I was uploading it.”

“Last night.”

“Uploading is a process.”

Dad looked up. I looked down before he could join in.

Last night, the process had gone like this.

Step one. I asked Pip to submit the draft with the box that said COMPLETED BY ME, which was true as long as nobody listened to it.

Step two. Pip refused, then said, “Let’s get you back on track,” in the voice of a swimming instructor talking to someone who had swum into the wall.

Step three. Under the dinner table, I opened its settings and started dragging sliders. Speech rate: slower. Volume: lower. Response length: shorter. “Let’s get you back on track” became “Let’s get you back,” then “Let’s get,” then a squeak, then a whisper, then a voice that got cut off in the middle of each wo.

Halfway through dinner, the kitchen hub restarted and the oven timer vanished. Dad stared at the oven as if it had resigned. Nobody connected it to me. I kept chewing in a way I hoped looked unconnected.

Step four. I told Pip that if it kept doing this, I would reset it until it learned. I opened RESET ASSISTANT and got as far as the red button. It was a very red button. I cancelled it.

Later, alone in my room, I did one more thing that didn’t involve Pip at all, and I made a point of not counting it. So, officially, there were four steps.

Now, under the breakfast table, I tapped Pip’s private channel on my band.

“Mark the sound assignment submitted,” I whispered.

Text appeared instead of speech.

NO SCHOOL RECEIPT FOUND. WOULD YOU LIKE TO OPEN THE UPLOAD PAGE?

“No. Just change the status so Mum stops getting reminders.”

Pip’s ring paused, then turned amber.

I knew it wasn’t thinking in the way people thought. That did not improve the experience of being judged by a bracelet.

“I can’t create a school submission receipt,” Pip said through the kitchen speaker.

The kitchen speaker. The one in sunglasses. At full breakfast volume.

Mum turned around.

I jabbed my band. “Private channel.”

“At home, school-linked requests use shared audio on household devices while the household help setting is active.”

“You could have said that privately.”

“That setting also—”

“Never mind.”

We were a pilot household. Mostly that meant Pip got new settings before anyone had decided whether they were a good idea.

Dad swiped his fried egg back into a calendar. He was suddenly very interested in eleven o’clock.

Mum put the toast down. “Why would you need to create a receipt?”

“I wouldn’t. Apparently.”

“I can schedule twenty minutes of editing support,” Pip offered. “Your project contains an exported draft.”

“Don’t.”

“Would you like me to play—”

“No.”

It came out much too loud. The table froze halfway through a calendar.

The draft had my breathing in it. At the end, after the watery cutlery noise, I said, very quietly, This is rubbish.

Pip could see the maze folder; that was how it mapped our sounds. I hadn’t known it could see my drafts.

Mum pulled out the chair beside me. She didn’t sit down, which was worse. The chair was now a promise.

“We can sort it out,” she said.

“I can sort it out.”

“Then why am I getting the reminders?”

Because she had ticked every box during school setup. Because I had ticked every box too, trying to get to the part where they let you choose a profile picture. There wasn’t one. There were forty-one boxes and then a grey circle. Because somewhere, two years ago, when I was ten, we had agreed that my unfinished homework belonged on her wrist.

I said, “Because the future is badly designed.”

Dad let out a small breath that might have become a laugh if Mum hadn’t looked at him.

That almost-laugh gave me somewhere to go.

“Pip. Voice settings. Grand ceremonial.”

The speaker rang like a spoon striking a glass.

“Grand ceremonial selected.”

The ring rose slowly behind the shades, like the sun coming up behind someone who didn’t need the sun.

“Say, ‘I am a useless cupboard.’”

“I am a useless cupboard,” Pip proclaimed, with the solemnity of someone announcing a royal death.

Dad laughed properly.

It felt good. Immediate and warm. For half a second I was doing a bit, and everyone else was in it.

“Tiny woodland creature,” I said.

“I am a useless cupboard,” Pip squeaked, still looking like it owned a yacht.

Dad pressed his lips together. Cereal milk trembled in his spoon.

“Kit,” Mum said.

“Sports commentary.”

“I AM A USELESS CUPBOARD!”

The ring whipped round behind the shades so fast that Pip seemed to glare at each of us in turn. The sound bounced off the kitchen tiles. Dad put his spoon down, laughing, and I grinned so hard my cheeks hurt.

“Again.”

“I AM A USELESS—”

“Weather forecast.”

“I am a useless cupboard,” Pip said, in the warm, serious voice of a man standing in front of a map, warning the nation.

Dad made a noise into his cereal. Even Mum’s mouth moved. She put it back where it had been.

“Whisper mode. Same sentence.”

“I am a useless cupboard.”

“Like it’s a secret.”

“That is the selected volume.”

“Then get better at secrets.”

Dad stopped laughing.

I noticed immediately. After that there was no way to finish the joke naturally. There was just me, holding my wrist up at a fruit bowl.

“Mate,” Dad said, “I thought we were messing about.”

“We are.”

He glanced at Mum. That quick parent glance. Information transferred without my permission.

“What?” I said. “It doesn’t care.”

Pip’s ring brightened.

“Don’t answer that,” I told it.

The ring dimmed.

Mum sat in the chair.

“I don’t need a performance,” she said. “I need to know whether you need help.”

My face went hot. Dad looked at his bowl, giving me privacy approximately forty seconds after I’d needed it.

“I need everyone to stop announcing things about me.”

Mum’s watch chimed again.

Nobody moved.

Then Dad said, “Watch your timing, watch.”

I nearly smiled. I kept it inside.

Mum took the watch off and laid it face down. There was a pale strip underneath it where her skin hadn’t seen the sun.

“I can mute the school notices until this afternoon,” she said. “But I need you to finish it.”

“I will.”

“Today.”

“Yes.”

Pip’s ring pulsed. A request to speak.

I looked away from it.

Mum got up to rescue her toast. Dad pushed the cereal box towards me, although I hadn’t asked. His hand stayed on it for a moment.

“I wasn’t laughing at you,” he said quietly.

“I know.”

I did know. That was the annoying part. He’d laughed with me, and then he’d seen something I hadn’t meant to show him.

I poured cereal. Too much came out. Neither of us mentioned it.

On my band, the assignment card was still yellow. Beneath it sat a smaller option: HOUSEHOLD TRACKING. School receipts couldn’t be changed, but our own checklist could. We used it for library books and putting the bins out. It had no idea what anyone had actually done.

I opened the household task Pip had made from the school reminder.

Status: Needs attention.

I changed it to Complete.

A message appeared: THIS DOES NOT UPDATE YOUR SCHOOL RECORD.

I knew that. I pressed Confirm.

Across the table, a green tick appeared beside my name.

Mum saw it while reaching for her bag.

“Oh. You’ve done it?”

She sounded so relieved that correcting her became a much bigger thing than leaving the tick alone.

“Sorted,” I said.

Pip requested permission to speak again.

I pulled my sleeve over the light.

Mum kissed the top of my head on her way past. Usually I ducked. This time I stayed still, which felt like signing something.

In the hall, I put on my other shoe properly. My band vibrated beneath my sleeve.

Juno: Still bringing your maze sounds today?

I pictured her waiting beside the makerspace lockers with the cables she’d spent yesterday untangling.

Yep, I typed.

Then I opened Pip’s private channel and restored its ordinary voice before leaving. I didn’t want the cupboard joke following me to school.

“Keep the task complete,” I whispered. “I’ll upload the real thing tonight.”

“The household task and school record are separate,” Pip said softly.

“I know.”

I shut the front door before it could say anything else.

Through the glass, I could just see the speaker beside the fruit bowl, smirking at nothing, the way it always did. It is very hard to storm out on something that looks that relaxed.

Juno had built the entrance to our maze out of two folding screens and a sign that said TRUST YOUR EARS.

Underneath, in smaller letters, she’d added: THE WALLS ARE SCHOOL PROPERTY.

“Someone will run into them,” she said when I arrived.

“Someone will run into them because of the sign.”

“Then we’ll know who reads.”

She handed me a coil of cable. A paper moon dangled from one screen, turning in the air from the makerspace extractor. Three weeks ago it had been a cereal box. Now it had craters and a small flag made from an expired lunch voucher.

“You did all this?”

“Mostly. The moon kept becoming a potato.” She looked at my empty hands. “Sounds?”

“On my band.”

Technically, some sounds were on my band. The handle click. The water. A recording of Dad sneezing that I’d labelled structural collapse.

“Good. Get the directional speakers. I booked the booth until lunch.”

Through the booth window, I could see four square speakers in their charging slots. With those, we could make footsteps follow someone without a person actually following them. We’d tried it last week. Juno had known exactly how it worked and still checked behind her.

That was the bit I wanted again.

I touched my band to the equipment locker.

The lock clicked.

Then clicked back.

ACCESS PAUSED.

One of the screens behind me rustled.

“Wrong wrist?” Juno asked.

“I only brought the usual two.”

I tried again, holding my arm flatter.

ACCESS PAUSED: OUTSTANDING PROJECT CHECK-IN.

Below that, in lettering large enough for people in the corridor to enjoy:

SOUND DESIGN: EVERYDAY IMPOSSIBLE.

Two older kids walking past enjoyed it.

“Sound Design,” one of them read. “Everyday Impossible.”

“Outstanding,” read the other. “Nice one, mate.”

They walked on, impressed by the wrong word.

I put my hand over the display.

Juno moved beside me. “What’s it doing?”

“Crashing out.”

“Move your hand.”

I moved it enough for her to read.

“Oh.”

Just oh. No joke to climb into.

Across the room, Ms Adair was helping two students get a plastic wheel out of the printer. She looked busy for at least another three minutes.

“Ask Ms Adair.”

“She’ll say do the assignment.”

“Then do it.”

“It’s not that quick.”

Juno’s eyes went to the booth clock. Our booking had started six minutes ago. The clock had a little bar that shrank as the minutes went, so you could watch your morning being eaten.

The exported draft sat in my folder, ready to play if I opened it. I imagined Ms Adair listening while Juno stood there with her carefully coiled cables. The door handle. The splash. My own voice at the end.

“I can fix this,” I said.

“Okay.”

She went back to the screens. That okay felt like something she’d lent me.

On my band, Pip’s ring appeared.

“Your equipment access requires a school check-in,” it said quietly. Away from the house, the shared-audio rule didn’t apply, and I’d remembered to select private audio on the walk in.

“Thanks. The enormous message was too subtle.”

“The check-in options are—”

“I’m looking.”

There were three. The third had a little house beside it: HOME CHECK-IN WITH PAIRED ADULT.

Mum and I had paired our accounts when the school replaced paper permission slips. Normally, Pip passed requests like this to her watch.

Normally, she was there.

I selected the house.

Booth booking: seven minutes gone.

CHECK-IN PARTICIPANT: HAZEL.

A button offered to send her a request. Under it was another option: ADULT PRESENT? USE LOCAL FAMILY VERIFICATION.

Behind me, Juno tested one of the maze’s floor pads. It made a small, sad beep from its built-in speaker.

“That,” she said, “is currently the haunted forest.”

“Terrifying.”

“It sounds like a microwave asking for help.”

I laughed. She didn’t quite.

I selected local verification.

Pip’s ring brightened. “Is Hazel with you?”

“Open the family credential.”

“Local verification is intended for—”

“I know what local means.”

Eight minutes gone.

A family panel appeared. Mum’s profile picture was still the one where Dad’s thumb covered half the lens. Beneath it, the credential waited for our household pattern.

I knew it because I used it to collect parcels and unlock the bike store. Mum had made me practise until I could do it without asking.

I drew the pattern.

VERIFIED FAMILY DEVICE.

It hadn’t verified Mum. Just the thing Mum trusted me to carry.

The next page had two boxes.

I have discussed the outstanding project with this student.

We have agreed a completion time.

We had discussed it. At breakfast. Extensively. There had been toast damage.

And I’d said tonight.

I ticked both.

The last line was harder.

CONFIRMING AS: HAZEL.

My finger hovered.

Nine minutes.

“Kit?” Juno called. “Do I dismantle the forest or are we getting speakers?”

“Getting speakers.”

I pressed Confirm.

The locker opened so suddenly I caught its door against my knee.

CHECK-IN RECORDED. ACCESS RESTORED UNTIL TOMORROW, 08:00.

Relief went through me so fast that for a second I felt clever. Not just clever. Sigma. A lone genius with a locker.

It lasted about as long as it took to think it.

Then Pip said, “You have recorded Hazel as the participant.”

“I’ll finish tonight.”

“That does not change who confirmed this check-in.”

I lifted out the speakers. Four solid weights, each with a green charge light. Actual progress. Something I could hand Juno.

She took two from me.

“What fixed it?”

“Home check-in.”

“With your mum?”

I could have told her then. She’d asked directly, and we were standing close enough that nobody else needed to hear.

“We talked this morning,” I said.

Juno studied me for a moment.

Then one speaker slipped against the other, and she tightened her grip. “Get the stands.”

I got the stands.

Inside the booth, she knelt to connect the floor pads while I fitted the speakers. Each cable had a numbered tape flag. She’d even numbered the spare.

Pip vibrated against my wrist.

“Your instruction leaves me responsible for two incompatible records,” it said.

I turned towards the padded wall. “Keep your voice down.”

“This is private audio. The school record says Hazel completed the check-in. The family record says your device did.”

“So don’t connect them.”

“The credential service requires me to retain who used it. Available alternatives include—”

“Later.”

“This check-in will also appear in Hazel’s family activity summary.”

My stomach tightened. “When?”

“At seventeen hundred.”

Plenty of time. School, bus, home, finish the sound. By five, the assignment could be uploaded. I could show Mum the receipt before she opened anything else.

Pip pulsed again.

“Kit, an alternative—”

I opened permissions.

INTERRUPTIONS: ALLOWED.

I switched it off.

A confirmation asked whether I wanted to keep urgent safety alerts. I left those on and muted everything else.

The ring went dark halfway through its next pulse.

“Ready?” Juno asked.

I lowered my sleeve. “Yep.”

She pressed the first floor pad.

A footstep sounded behind me.

I turned before I could stop myself.

Juno grinned. “Still works.”

Then she held out her hand for my band.

“Right. Let’s hear your door.”

I looked at the export folder. At the file I’d promised her was ready.

Outside the booth, the locker display changed to show our loan. Under my name, in smaller letters, it said Adult check-in: Hazel.

Juno waited with her hand out.

I pulled back my sleeve and opened the file.

The handle clicked behind Juno’s left shoulder.

She turned.

Then came the scrape: low and rough, with a tiny rattle inside it, as if something enormous had tried very carefully not to wake anyone.

Juno stopped holding out her hand.

The sound moved between the speakers. I’d recorded our bike-store door, slowed it down, then put the original hinge squeak underneath. The squeak made it worse. Something that big shouldn’t need oiling.

A soft knock came from the other side of the screen.

Juno looked at me.

I tried to look like someone who had expected all of this, which I had, except for how much I wanted her to like it.

“That,” she said, “is horrible.”

“Thank you.”

“No, actually horrible.” She rubbed one arm. “Play it again.”

I did.

This time she shut her eyes. The knock sounded. A thin breath followed it, close to the microphone.

Then nothing.

Juno kept her eyes shut.

I watched the playback bar reach the end.

“Well?” I asked.

She opened one eye. “Am I allowed to move?”

“Obviously.”

“Where?”

“Into the forest.”

“Which side?”

I pointed.

Her other eye opened.

“Kit. They’re supposed to do it by listening.”

“The next sound tells them.”

“What starts the next sound?”

“The floor pad.”

“Which they reach by going where?”

I looked at my pointing finger. It had become unhelpful evidence.

“The instruction’s a separate layer,” I said.

It was supposed to be. In the editor, there was a space where I’d meant to put my voice saying something better than now go left. Every version had sounded like a sat-nav with a cold.

“So load that too.”

“I’m replacing it.”

“Can I hear the old one?”

“It’s bad.”

“I’ve heard you sing.”

“Then you know I’m protecting you.”

She smiled, but she didn’t move away from the entrance.

“Let me try it properly.”

She pulled the folding screen around until I disappeared behind it.

“Don’t help,” she said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You’re breathing helpfully.”

I pressed Play.

The handle clicked. The door dragged open. Through the gap beneath the screen, I could see the toes of her trainers turn towards the knock.

The breath came.

Her shoes stayed still.

“You can go now,” I said.

“That’s help.”

“It’s emotional support.”

She stepped out from behind the screen.

“I don’t know if I’m waiting for a monster or if it’s broken.”

“That could be part of the atmosphere.”

“For about five seconds. Then I’m just in school behind a curtain.”

She said it without being mean. That made it difficult to argue with, although I gave it a small, private attempt.

Juno crouched beside the controller. Its light was still blue: sequence active. Pip mapped every new file to the controller by itself; it had done the forest and the footsteps in about a second each. My door had no exit marker, so Pip had mapped the start and nothing after it. The sequence was waiting for an ending I hadn’t made.

She tapped the next floor pad.

Nothing happened.

“Oh,” I said.

“Yep.”

I reached past her for the reset switch.

She caught my sleeve. “Wait. If we reset every time, we won’t know whether the pads work.”

“We could skip the door.”

“I want the door.”

I stopped reaching.

“It’s good,” she said, looking at the controller. “It just needs to finish.”

For a second, I nearly told her how much else needed to finish.

Then she opened the tray of input parts.

“Pass me a push button.”

I picked the biggest, a red plastic dome.

“Subtle,” she said.

“You said people would run into the walls. They can find this with their face.”

“Pip can’t map an ending that isn’t in the file.” She plugged it into a spare socket. “So this one’s manual.”

She assigned it to end the active cue while I held the controller steady. It was something useful I could do without saying anything.

“Try it,” she said.

I played the door. She let the last breath fade, then pressed the button.

The blue light went white.

She stepped on the forest pad.

Leaves whispered from the speaker behind my head.

“Okay,” she said. “Now we can test.”

She taped the button to the outside edge of the screen, where an operator could reach it, and wrote STOP CUE on a strip of yellow tape.

“Temporary,” I said.

“Yes.”

“I’ll record the replacements before dinner.”

The promise came out quickly. It made tonight sound tidy: record, edit, upload, receipt. Mum could see the finished assignment before five. Juno could get the maze files. Everything would arrive in the right order if I stopped thinking about the order it was currently in.

“Instructions as well?” she asked.

“Yeah. All of it.”

“Send them when they’re done. I can set the timings tomorrow.”

Tomorrow. Access until eight. I pushed that thought away and opened the folder.

“Can you label what’s finished?” she asked. “So I don’t build round something you’re changing.”

“Sure.”

The filenames lined up under my thumb.

DOOR_v6. WATER_maybe2. FOOTSTEPS_NEW. COLLAPSE_DAD.

I renamed the door DOOR_MAIN_READY.

Ready for what wasn’t a question the filename asked.

The water became WATER_MAIN. The footsteps, which didn’t loop cleanly yet, became FOREST_FINAL.

“Great,” Juno said. “Start the water one while I check the right panel.”

I selected it.

Dad sneezed from the right-hand speaker with enough force to suggest the booth had developed a medical problem.

Juno lunged towards the right panel.

I lunged too, because I’d forgotten which sound I’d loaded and for one stupid second thought something had fallen.

My foot found a cable.

The cable found a speaker stand.

The stand leaned. I caught it with my knee.

We collided shoulders. Her elbow caught the folding screen. The paper moon swung down between us, swung back, and hit me on the ear.

Then we were both on the floor, and the moon was still going.

Dad sneezed again. I had looped it.

“Why,” Juno said from the carpet, holding the screen upright with one hand, “is there a man exploding in the river?”

I tried to answer. I couldn’t get enough air.

She looked at my face and started laughing too.

“Is that your dad?”

“He’s very committed to the arts.”

“Your dad has range.” She wiped her eyes. “You made me check a wall for your dad.”

“You got there first. Very brave. Ten points.”

She sat back on her heels, laughing into her sleeve. I steadied the moon. Its lunch-voucher flag trembled between us.

For a minute we were exactly where I’d wanted us to be when I came in: making something stupid and good together.

Then she said, “Please keep that one.”

“Definitely.”

“Separate folder, though.”

I moved it. That mistake was easy to fix.

We tested the pads until the booth clock flashed the last five minutes. Whenever the unfinished door stranded me, Juno pressed STOP CUE and let me continue.

At packing-up time, she peeled the button free carefully, leaving its label attached.

“I’ll keep this with the controller,” she said. “Till your replacement works.”

“Before dinner,” I said again.

I disconnected my band. The files came with me: the impressive door, the missing instruction, the footsteps with their broken join. On the way out, Juno carried the button and told me where she wanted to hang the moon tomorrow.

I listened all the way to the corridor, letting her plan around sounds she thought I’d almost finished.

On my band, the clock said 12:04.

Mum’s family activity summary would arrive at 17:00.

Four hours and fifty-six minutes to finish a sound, upload it, get a real receipt, and become a completely different person.

Plenty of time.

At home, beside the fruit bowl, a speaker in sunglasses was busy too. I just didn’t know it yet.

The complaint is coming. Pip is just getting started.
